Fundamentals, explained

What Is a P/E Ratio?

The price tag on a dollar of profit — and why it matters before you invest.

So what is it, exactly?

Picture this: two coffee shops are for sale on the same street. Both earn $50,000 a year in profit. One is priced at $500,000, the other at $1.5 million. Same profit, very different price tags. Which one is the better deal? That question — how much am I paying for each dollar of profit? — is exactly what the P/E ratio answers.

P/E stands for price-to-earnings. You take a company's stock price and divide it by its earnings per share. A P/E of 10 means you're paying $10 for every $1 the company earns each year. A P/E of 30 means you're paying $30 for that same dollar.

Why should you care?

Because a great company can still be a bad deal at the wrong price. The P/E ratio is the fastest way to tell whether a stock is priced like a bargain, priced fairly, or priced for perfection. It's not the whole story — fast-growing companies often deserve higher P/Es — but it's the first question a careful investor asks.

One friendly warning: a low P/E isn't automatically good. Sometimes a stock is cheap because the business is in trouble. That's why P/E is one of eight checks — never the only one.

The grading scale

Let's make it real

Imagine two companies that each earn $5 per share every year. Company A's stock costs $50. Company B's stock costs $150. Same earnings — three times the price.

Company A $50 price ÷ $5 earnings
P/E 10
You pay $10 for each $1 of yearly profit.
Company B $150 price ÷ $5 earnings
P/E 30
You pay $30 for each $1 of yearly profit.

Is Company B overpriced? Maybe — or maybe investors expect its earnings to grow fast enough to justify it. The P/E tells you what the market is charging. The other seven checks help you decide if it's worth paying.
